procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders passed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate under s. 18(1) of the Suppression of Immoral Traffic in Women and Girls Act, 1956 with respect to certain premises.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondents challenged the validity of Section 18 in the Punjab High Court, Circuit Bench at Delhi. The High Court held that Section 18 violated Article 14 of the Constitution when action is taken independently of Section 7. The High Court allowed the petitions (Criminal Writs Nos. 3-D, 4-D, 5-D, 6-D, 7-D, 10-D and 12-D of 1962) and quashed the notices issued to the respondents. They also quashed the order refusing to raise the attachment in respect of flat No. 54.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appeals were brought to the Supreme Court on the strength of certificates issued by the High Court of Punjab. The first appellant in these appeals, Shri A. C. Aggarwal, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Delhi, appealed the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court upheld the conclusions reached by the High Court, but on different grounds. The Supreme Court held that the Magistrate should have first taken action under s.3 before proceeding under s.18. The appeals failed and were dismissed.

directions: The learned magistrate is not debarred from taking fresh proceedings against the respondents in accordance with law as explained by the court.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 18 of the Act is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution on the ground that it discriminates against the accused by providing a different procedure than a regular trial.

facts: The case concerned whether Section 18 of the Act was unconstitutional because it allowed for a summary procedure (a 'hearing' before a magistrate regarding the use of a premises) for a situation that could also be subject to a regular criminal trial under Sections 3 or 7 of the same Act.
The argument against the law was that this gave authorities an arbitrary choice between two widely different procedures for the same set of facts, which amounted to discrimination under Article 14.
The High Court had accepted this argument and found Section 18 to be unconstitutional.
law: Article 14 of the Constitution prohibits discrimination and guarantees equality before the law.

A law is not considered discriminatory if it creates different procedures for different classes of cases, provided that the classification is reasonable and has a rational relationship to the objective of the law.
application: The Supreme Court distinguished between the proceedings under Sections 3 and 7 and the proceedings under Section 18.
It reasoned that Sections 3 and 7 deal with punishing *persons* for committing offences, whereas Section 18 deals with the *premises* being used for immoral traffic.

The Court found that the facts required to be proven are not identical. To secure a conviction under Sections 3 or 7, the prosecution must establish the accused's intention or knowledge. However, for action under Section 18, intent and knowledge are not necessary ingredients.

Based on this distinction, the Court held that the Act creates two distinct classes of cases: (1) those involving the prosecution of a person under Section 3 or 7, and (2) those involving action against the premises under Section 18.
The Court concluded that this classification is reasonable and directly relates to the Act's objective of suppressing immoral traffic.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge, holding that Section 18 is not violative of Article 14. The Court found that the section deals with a distinct class of cases (action against premises) that is different from the criminal prosecution of persons under Sections 3 or 7. This classification was deemed reasonable and therefore constitutionally valid.

issue.issue_text: Whether a magistrate can ignore a cognizable offence disclosed under Section 3 of the Act and have recourse to Section 18, thereby depriving the parties of the benefit of a regular trial and appeal.

facts: The police reports made available to the court clearly disclosed that the respondents had committed cognizable offenses under Section 3 of the Act.
law: Section 3 of the Act is a penal provision that provides for punishment for keeping a brothel, which requires a regular trial and allows for an appeal if convicted.
Section 18 of the Act is a preventive measure dealing with premises, which involves a more summary procedure.

Under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a magistrate is bound to take cognizance of any cognizable offense brought to their notice. The Court interprets the phrase "may take cognizance" to mean "must take cognizance" to avoid violating Article 14 of the Constitution.
application: The Court performed a "harmonious construction" of the Act's provisions to determine the correct procedure.
It reasoned that a magistrate cannot choose to ignore a cognizable offense (under Section 3) and instead use the summary procedure under Section 18.

To do so would unlawfully deprive the accused parties of the significant benefits of a regular trial, including the right to cross-examine witnesses, present evidence, and the right to appeal a conviction.

The Court established a clear procedural order: the magistrate must first proceed against the accused under the penal provisions of Section 3. Only after that case is disposed of can the magistrate initiate preventive action under Section 18, if there is a reason for it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the magistrate's proceedings were not in accordance with the law. A magistrate cannot ignore a disclosed cognizable offense under Section 3 and proceed only under Section 18, as this would deny the accused their right to a regular trial and appeal. The magistrate must first take action under the penal provision (Section 3) before considering the preventive measure (Section 18).

arguments.issue_text: Whether a magistrate can ignore a cognizable offence disclosed under Section 3 of the Act and have recourse to Section 18, thereby depriving the parties of the benefit of a regular trial and appeal.
appellant_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the appellant's argument, but it can be inferred from the magistrate's actions that they argued a magistrate has the discretion to proceed under Section 18 even if a cognizable offence under Section 3 is disclosed in the police reports.
respondent_arguments: When police reports disclose a cognizable offence under Section 3 of the Act, the magistrate cannot ignore it and proceed under Section 18.
Proceeding directly under Section 18 deprives the parties of the benefit of a regular trial and the right of appeal.
Under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the magistrate is bound to take cognizance of any cognizable offence brought to his notice and has no discretion in the matter.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statutory classification that is reasonable and provides for distinct classes of cases is not unconstitutional. However, where a report discloses a cognizable offense under Section 3 of the Act, a magistrate cannot ignore that offense and proceed under Section 18; action must first be taken under Section 3.
obiter: Reasonable classification is permitted but must be based upon some real and substantial distinction bearing a reasonable and just relation to the objective of the classification.
The presumption is always in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment, as it must be assumed the legislature understands the needs of its people and its laws are based on adequate grounds.
If a law deals equally with all members of a well-defined class, it is not open to the charge of denial of equal protection.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that while Section 18 of the Act is not unconstitutional, the proceedings taken by the magistrate were not in accordance with the law. When police reports disclose a cognizable offense under Section 3, the magistrate cannot ignore it and proceed directly under the preventive measures of Section 18. The magistrate must first take cognizance of the criminal offense before any other action can be taken.
legal_tests_applied: For an Article 14 challenge, a law is not unconstitutional if it deals equally with all of a certain well-defined class. Reasonable classification is permitted, but it must be based upon some real and substantial distinction bearing a reasonable and just relation to the object of the legislation.
There is a presumption in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment.

Under Section 190(1)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, when a police report discloses a cognizable offense, a magistrate is bound to take action and cannot ignore it in favor of a different proceeding.
why_appellant_lost: The magistrate acted unlawfully by ignoring a cognizable offense disclosed in the police reports. The reports disclosed a cognizable offence under s. 3 of the Act and in such a case the magistrate cannot ignore the cognizable offence and merely have recourse to s. 18.
The magistrate's procedural error deprived the respondents of significant rights. By proceeding directly under Section 18, the magistrate was 'dep~iving parties of the benefit Qf a trial and appeal'.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed with the respondent's central procedural argument that when police reports disclose a cognizable offense under Section 3, the magistrate is obligated to take cognizance of it and cannot simply resort to the preventive measures in Section 18.

The court found that the magistrate's failure to follow the correct procedure rendered the proceedings against the respondents invalid, stating 'the proceedings taken by the learned magistrate against the respondents are not in accordance with law as he has proceeded against them under s.18 without first taking action under s.3.'
policy_considerations: The court distinguished between the purpose of different sections of the Act, noting that Sections 3 and 7 are punitive ('punishment of persons guilty of the offences'), whereas Section 18 is a 'preventive measure' and 'in no sense a prosecution.'
The purpose of Article 14's equal protection clause is 'to prevent any person or class of persons from being singled out as a special subject for discrimination and hostile treatment.'
